chapters.title: Flower
chapters.content:
King of Death

My head hurt.

I clearly remembered falling asleep last night in the spring rain,
but my stomach burned and my throat was dry.

I'm pretty sure I ate rat poison and died yesterday.
So why am I opening my eyes?

Just then, someone called out,

"Darin! Don't you have class today?"

I thought,

What kind of class would a cat have?

And then—

Oh. That was a dream.

I jumped out of bed.

After stretching, I walked into the living room.
Mom had made a honey-ginger ade
and set it on the table.

I started drinking it.
Kept drinking it.

"Mom, how did I get home last night?"

"How else?
Your professor called, so your father went and brought you back.
You're all grown up—how much did you drink
that all your friends ran away
and the professor had to call?"

The moment she said that, I realized—

Ah. My life.
This is the greatest humiliation of my existence.

I washed up in a hurry and headed to school.

As soon as I arrived,
my classmates from the same department—Minyoung and Songhwa—
started laughing the moment they saw my face.

"Darin!!! Are you okaaay~?
Strawberry candy, pleeease~~~
Aaah~"

They laughed as they said it.

I brushed it off vaguely.

"When did I ever...?"

Minyoung shot back.

"When?
You seriously don't remember yesterday?

We went to karaoke,
you were screaming songs at the top of your lungs...
then suddenly climbed onto the table and started dancing.
You don't remember that?"

Songhwa continued,

"And then you called the KOD professor
and started arguing with him,
asking what you'd done so wrong—
then you started crying.

So we called the professor,
and he actually came.
He showed up."

Minyoung laughed even harder.

"When the professor arrived, you said this—remember?

'King of Death came to me? Are you Yeomra?
So I'm dead now? You son of a bitch!

Why do you give me an F every single exam?
That's why everyone calls you
an unmarried old bachelor with hysteria!'

You seriously said all that.

Congrats—your F for this semester
is basically confirmed."

That's when it hit me.

This is bad.

No—
this is really bad.

I already had three F's
in required major courses.

I barely had time to prepare for a job as it was,
and the thought of retaking classes
during senior-year field training
made everything go dark.

Bribe

I thought to myself.

If I get on Inside KOD's bad side,
I'm really finished.

The seniors who still hadn't graduated after nine semesters
all said the same thing.

Never take his class.

He's from our department,
has solved and published the answers to every subject,
and yet somehow makes even the most brilliant students
decide—on their own—
that they have no talent.

They said he wasn't even human.
That he belonged to the realm of gods.

I thought they were just exaggerating.

I'd been good at math since I was a kid.
Basically a genius.
Hmph.

Then came the day I received his exam paper,
and I realized—

this wasn't exaggeration.

"Explain the infinity of the universe using mathematics."

I couldn't write a single word.

I couldn't tell
whether this was math,
philosophy,
or physics.

I thought I was confident,
but in front of that question—
as if it were quietly mocking me—
I realized I was nothing.

Still, I made up my mind.

At least this semester,
I had to avoid an F.

I would go to him properly,
apologize for what happened yesterday,
and clearly state—logically—
that grading based on emotion
was a violation of academic rules.

And yet—

for some reason,
there was a caramel macchiato in my hand.

This is not the hand of logic...

Each step toward the professor's office
felt three times heavier than usual.

On the door, a sign read: IN OFFICE.

That alone felt ominous.

I knocked and went in, tense.

Inside sat
the KOD—
and beside him,
a professor from the philosophy department.
peacefully seated side by side.

The KOD asked,

"Student. What brings you here?"

Without thinking,
I held out the coffee.

"I think I made a mistake yesterday.
I came to apologize."

He took the cup
and stared at it for a long moment.

"Caramel macchiato."

He nodded.

"A rather emotional choice."

At that moment,
my heart turned completely blank—
like an unanswered exam paper.

"Anything else?"

I carefully said the words
I had prepared.

"I believe emotion and reason
should be kept separate."

The philosophy professor let out a small laugh.

"How classical."

The KOD smiled,
as if he had been waiting for that.

"A good thought."

Then, in a perfectly calm voice,
he added,

"There was, after all,
an answer you were looking for yesterday.

Strawberry candy."

As if nothing mattered,
he set the cup down and continued.

"I'll tell you the answer to the final exam.
The answer is

Unmarried old bachelor with hysteria.

You know that even one wrong letter
means an F."

The philosophy professor nodded approvingly.

"A very philosophical answer.
It suits you."

"Indeed... quite symbolic."

My face burned.

I don't remember what I said after that.
I fled the office, almost running.

This semester, too,
my F was confirmed.

On my way home,
I suddenly realized—

my backpack was gone.

Damn it...

"I left it in the professor's office."

I went back.

I knocked.

The door opened just a crack.

No one came out—
only my backpack slid into view.

From inside, a voice said,

"Here for this?"

I grabbed it and replied automatically,

"Yes. Thank you."

The door closed
without another word.

That day marked
the absolute peak
of humiliation in my life.

Repetition

When I went to the department office,
Minyoung and Songhwa were there.

They looked at me with obvious curiosity.

"So... did you sort out that KOD thing?"
Minyoung asked.
"How did it go?"

I sighed and said,

"Do you really think that professor is the kind of person
things just get 'sorted out' with?"

That only made them more curious.

"Why? Why? Why?"
Songhwa leaned in.
"What did you do? How bad was it?"

I waved it off.

"If you'd seen it—
no. Never mind. Let's not talk about it.
I'm feeling gloomy.
Let's just go eat dinner."

And with that, we left
and went to a restaurant near campus.

After that,
I remember nothing.

My head hurt.

I felt strangely irritated,
like something was off.
I thought I smelled something.
My stomach churned.

Then my mom came in.

"Honestly... I raised you all this way,
and all you do is drink every day.
Your father got another call from your professor
and went out to bring you home again.
What a disgrace...

Anyway—
can you even go to your teaching practicum next semester?"

I snapped awake.

"Mom—what did you say?
Professor?
Dad?"

She answered calmly,

"Yes. Yesterday again.
You were completely out of it.
Minyoung called.

When your father went out,
you were holding onto your professor's arm,
crying, then laughing,
then throwing a tantrum.

He said he was so embarrassed and apologetic
that he basically dragged you home and ran."

I froze.

"Yesterday... again?
Me?
I called the professor?

I'm doomed.
How am I supposed to go to school now?"

Mom frowned.

"Why would you go to school?
It's Saturday.

I made hangover soup.
Come out and eat."

Mom sighed and added,
"Honestly...
you're already a senior.
Don't you even have a boyfriend?
How do you manage not to date even once?"

I froze under the blanket.

Boyfriend?

As if I had time for that.

As if anyone would date someone
who argues with professors about infinity
and curses them in karaoke rooms.

I kicked the blanket harder.

"Ugh—
this is so embarrassing!"

She left the room.

I pulled the blanket over my head
and, without realizing it,
started kicking it with my feet.

"Ugh—
this is so embarrassing!"

Open Book

I made up my mind.

Embarrassment only lasts a moment.

Once I got through the final exams of my third year, second semester,
I'd finally be done with these exhausting major courses.

So whenever I saw the KOD professor,
I didn't even say hello.
I just walked past him.

When the final exam notice went up,
I felt relief for the first time.

Open book.

We were allowed to open our books during the exam.

Ah... I survived.

Everyone already looked like they'd done the math.
Summary notes, highlighters, Post-its—
their textbooks were packed with color.
The entire department turned into a small library.

Even as I packed my books,
something felt off.

KOD!
was not the type to give a kind exam.

On the day of the test,

when we were told we could open our books,
everyone flipped pages at the same time.
The sound of paper filled the room.

Then we received the exam sheet.

I read the first line
and closed my book.

"OPEN BOOK."

The question was:

"Explain why the ladder game always results in a one-to-one correspondence."

I held my pen
and thought for a long time.

I considered opening the book again,
then stopped.

What kind of nonsense is this?

I drew a ladder game.
It was one-to-one.
No matter how I drew it,
it was always one-to-one.

What came to mind was:

This lunatic... all the way to the end.

And—

the sentence I'd heard in the professor's office
a few days earlier.

I thought for two hours
and then wrote my answer.

Unmarried old bachelor with hysteria.

I put my pen down.

After the exam,
people compared answers.

"What page did you use?"
"Which chapter was this from?"

Someone asked me,

"What did you write?"

I didn't answer.
No one would've believed me anyway.

The grades came out sooner than expected.

A+.

I stared at the screen for a long time
and checked again.

No mistake.
It was an A+.

The next day,
there was a commotion in front of the department office.

People were gathered around,
and a white sheet of paper
was posted on the central bulletin board.

〈OPEN BOOK – Model Answer〉

Below it
was my name.

Kim Darin

And beneath that,
just one line.

Unmarried old bachelor with hysteria.

Someone said,

"This... is the answer?"

Some laughed.
Some cursed.
Some took pictures.

"This is philosophy."
"No, it's just an insult to the professor."
"Then what were we doing?"

I wasn't standing there.

From a distance,
I glanced at the board once
and turned away.

At the end of the hallway,
KOD was walking
with the philosophy professor.

The philosophy professor said,

"A truly excellent text."

KOD nodded.

"It's open book."

He stopped for a moment,
looked at the board,
and said quietly,

"The answer is always public."

I stopped by a convenience store
and bought a strawberry candy.

I put it in my mouth
and slowly chewed.

For some reason,
it tasted a little sweet.

Typhoon

After the exam ended,
something about the department felt off.

I was summoned by one of the senior graduate assistants.
The moment she saw me, she said,

"Do you even have a brain, or not?
Everyone told you the professor was strange
and that you should avoid him if possible.
So why would you take his class anyway
and then turn in an exam
with an insult to the professor written on it?
What kind of student does that?"

The way my classmates looked at me had changed too.
Whenever I passed by,
their conversations stopped.

What hurt more
was Minyoung and Songhwa, my closest friends.
They didn't say anything,
but I could tell.

They thought
I had flirted with the professor
to get a good grade.

Suddenly,
it felt like the world had turned its back on me.

Then
the student representative gathered opinions
and submitted an official complaint
to the student affairs office and the professor.

KOD
posted a notice on the department bulletin board.

"Anyone dissatisfied with the exam, the grading,
or any related matter
will be given an opportunity
for a retest or regrading.

November 30, 10:00 a.m.
Room 305."

The student representative and the students
waited for the day
with the attitude that they had nothing to lose.

On the day itself,
students from the math department—
from first-years to seniors,
even graduate assistants—filled the room.
There weren't enough chairs,
so most people stood in the back.

I was afraid of people's eyes too,
but I was curious about what would happen,
so I sat down.

As soon as the professor entered,
he went to the board.

The professor walked in and wrote a large H on the board.

Rotated it 90 degrees.

"It's a function, isn't it?"

He left.

Silence.

The teaching assistant muttered, "College students who don't even know what a function is—" and walked out shaking his head.

We shuffled out like rain-soaked puppies, deflated and wordless.

From the next day on,
I went to school
and began studying the professor's solutions
and his research papers.

Only then did I see
how long he thought about a single problem,
how relentlessly
he held onto it.

I cried,
quietly.

Hazing

Minyoung and Songhwa were no longer my friends.

My classmates eventually apologized, saying they had misunderstood things,
but by then my heart had already turned away.

That wasn't the real problem, though.

The real problem was KOD

started looking... oddly impressive.

I kept thinking I should talk to him.
Say something smart.
Pretend I knew what I was doing.

Then I'd snap back to myself and think,
What the hell is wrong with me?

So I decided I'd ask him the hardest question in the major textbook.

I spent my days drifting between the library and the TA office, studying.
Every time I hit a wall in a proof,
I hunted down the proofs he had written.

Sometimes I felt a jolt of clarity.
Sometimes awe—
So that's how you do it.

And sometimes suspicion—
Wait. He solved this? That guy?

After two months, I reached a single conclusion:

I had no talent.

At this level, there was no way I could survive student teaching next semester.

So I decided to give up on the department.
Or transfer.

I was confident in physics.
Computer science, too.

When I asked the seniors in the TA office, they told me
the professor's approval was required.

So I went straight to his office.

Even though it was vacation, the door sign said IN OFFICE.

I knocked and went in.

He was playing online Go.

"Professor—"

"Hold on. Critical moment."

So I waited.

"Just a second," he'd said.
That second turned into thirty minutes.

After an hour, I called out again.

"Professor—?"

He was asleep.

"Oh! Sorry. I nodded off," he said cheerfully.
"Have a seat on the sofa."

He walked over to the coffee machine.

"Want coffee?
Or—how about soju?"

My face turned bright red.

"C-coffee, please."

He handed me a cup and said,

"So. What brings you here today?
Exams are over."

I answered,

"Professor, I don't think I have any talent for math.
I want to transfer."

He replied,

"No talent, huh...
Well, that part's true."

Then he smiled.

"But there's a condition."

I blinked.

"What kind of condition?"

He pulled out his phone and made a call.

"Hey. It's me.
How've you been?
Yeah, yeah.
So one of your juniors from my department wants to transfer.
What do you think?"

He handed me the phone.

"Hello?" I said.

"This little punk—
bringing shame to her father, what the hell do you think you're doing?!"

It was my dad.

"Why aren't you home already?!"

His voice boomed through the office like a loudspeaker.

Mortified, I hung up immediately.

When I gave the phone back, the professor said,

"Student Gadarine.
I am your senior—
from elementary school, middle school, high school, and college."

He leaned back.

"From today on, I'll treat you strictly as my junior.
Understood?"

"From now on, you answer within three seconds."

"Math is hard. Three."

"Yes, sir!"

"Math is filthy hard. Three."

"Yes, sir!"

"Impressive!"

"A senior's words are the words of heaven. Three."

"Of course, sir!"

"A senior ranks higher than mathematics itself. Three."

"No doubt, sir!"

"And yet—you put in less effort than your senior. Correct?"

"Yes, sir!"

"For the rest of this break,
you will come to my office every day.
You will study.
And you will take an exam every single day."

"Three. Two—"

"Yes, sir!!"

"Very good."

"Student Gadarine, go home and rest today.
Starting tomorrow, you report here. Three."

"Yes, sir!!"

That's how I became
the professor's lab rat.

Hard Training

Before I even realized what was happening,
a sudden countdown—three, two, one—
had me answering nothing but,
"Yes, sir!"

And just like that,
I stepped through the gates of a hell
I could no longer turn back from.

There was no way I could show up the next day
and say I couldn't do it.
That would be far too embarrassing.

No matter how notorious the KOD is, I thought,
he wouldn't actually kill me... right?
Only then did I finally fall asleep.

I woke to the sound of my alarm
and rushed to the professor's office as fast as I could.

"You're not at the level to be here yet,"
the professor said flatly.
"There's an empty desk left in the TA room.
Study there.

Your assignment is simple.
Set theory—from page one to the very last page.
Solve everything.

No time limit."

At first, the problems went smoothly.
But about a fifth of the way in,
there were one or two I couldn't solve.

Whenever I went to the professor with a question,
he would check my solution process and say,
"Go back and study this chapter again."

No matter how many times I tried,
when I returned with the same problem unsolved,
he would only say,
"Start from the previous chapter."

After about a week of this,
I finally understood why.

The reason I couldn't solve those problems
wasn't the problems themselves—
it was that I hadn't properly understood
the chapters before them.

Only then did I grasp
why the professor had forced such relentless repetition.

By the final chapter of set theory,
there was exactly one problem I couldn't crack.
I spent an entire week stuck on it.

No matter how hard I thought,
the answer wouldn't come.

Then one day,
as I sat absentmindedly on the toilet,
something suddenly clicked.

I threw on my clothes,
ran straight to the professor's office,
flung open the door,
and shouted,

"I think I finally understand
why the universe is infinite!"

The professor didn't even look at me.
He was calmly brewing coffee.

Without realizing it,
I walked up behind him
and wrapped my arms around his back.

A back hug.

He didn't seem particularly bothered.

"That's a bit aggressive for a eureka moment,"
he said mildly.
"Still rather clumsy with the grooming, aren't you?

Is that why they call you
Little Groom?"

Only then did I let go, startled.

"I'm sorry.
I'm so sorry..."

I bowed repeatedly
and retreated back to the TA room.

It was embarrassing.
Again.

That night, lying in bed,
replaying the day over and over,
I kicked the blankets in mortification.

There's no way I actually like
that hysterical old bachelor,
I told myself.
I was just thinking too deeply
and got carried away.

With that excuse,
I finally fell asleep.

And just like that,
the special winter break training
came to an end.


Refrigerator

My parents were born in neighboring rural villages

and went to the same school.

They were classmates, friends—

and eventually, husband and wife.

They got married right after graduating high school

and had me soon after,
so there's only a nineteen-year age gap between us.

Whenever there's a reunion or a gathering with old friends,

they always go together.

Sometimes, watching them mingle with their friends,

they bicker playfully over who's known whom longer.
It's oddly entertaining—
and genuinely warm.

Because they share the same memories, games, and friends,

there's never any room for unnecessary misunderstandings.

One Friday evening,

the two of them went out to dinner with friends.
I heard the sound of a taxi pulling up around three in the morning.
I figured that was that and went back to sleep.

The next morning,

I walked into the living room
and saw two people sleeping side by side on the floor—
my parents' friend was there.

I was thirsty.

I opened the refrigerator to grab some water.

The moment I did,

a horrible stench hit me,
and before I could stop myself, I screamed.

"KYAAAA—!"

Startled by my scream,

my parents stumbled out half-awake
and came over.

After checking the fridge,

my dad said casually,
"Oh. Looks like our friend peed in here."

My mom immediately shook him awake.

"Hey—wake up."

The friend groggily sat up.

"What's going on?"

He shuffled over to the refrigerator,

took a look inside,
and laughed shamelessly.

"Who the hell did this?"

That—

that was the professor's real self?

Impossible.

That meticulous, cold-blooded man...?

The professor spoke up.

"I always felt bad that I never got you a wedding gift.

I'll buy you one this time.
Let's go pick it out later.

But first—

let's get some hangover soup."

My parents laughed for a while, then nodded.

"Yeah, let's eat first.

Nothing's open at this hour anyway.

Darin, order four bowls of hangover soup on your phone."

While we waited for the food,

my dad cleaned out the refrigerator,
and my mom and the professor
sat together browsing refrigerators on their phones.

After breakfast,

we waited a bit.

Thankfully, by that evening,

a refrigerator installation technician arrived
and replaced it with a brand-new one—
a top-of-the-line model,
complete with a display panel and water purifier.

The professor stood up.

"Well, I should get going."

My mom stopped him.

"Eating dinner alone is lonely.

Why don't you stay and have dinner with us?"

He paused.

"Oh?

Sure."

He sat back down on the sofa.

We drank again.

And he didn't leave

until the following evening.

Go-Stop

In Korea, there's an extremely addictive card game called Go-Stop.
It's technically illegal gambling,
but when friends get together
or families play it casually during the holidays,
people tend to look the other way.

After the professor's visit to our house,
my parents began inviting him over from time to time on weekends,
saying that eating alone looked lonely.

He would show up in a tracksuit,
throw a jumper over it,
eat with us, drink a little,
and leave after sharing old stories.

One day,
my dad started talking about how he'd once gotten caught
playing Go-Stop in middle school
and had been scolded badly for it.

That was all it took.
An unplanned Go-Stop game began.

I joined in too.
By chance, I was sitting right behind the professor.

And somehow—
I was the only one losing.
Over and over.

No matter how we played,
I was the only one bleeding points.

I got irritated
and took a quick glance at the professor's hand.

He was throwing out completely strange cards—
which explained why I kept losing.

Without thinking, I blurted out,
"How can you play that card at that timing?"

My mom snapped,
"Hey. You don't look at other people's hands."

I shot back,
"Mom, try being in my position.
Professor, you don't actually know how to play Go-Stop, do you?"

The professor answered calmly,
"Isn't it just matching pictures and collecting sets?"

I lost it.

"That's how elementary school kids play!
You really have nothing you're good at
except math!!!"

I stormed into my room
and collapsed onto my bed.

Even then,
the laughter outside didn't stop.

No wonder he never got married,
I thought bitterly.

After dinner, the professor went home.
Later, I asked my mom,

"Was he kind of slow back when you were all in school?"

She looked at me like I was ridiculous.

"Does he really seem that way to you?
If he wanted to, he could've beaten all of us easily.
He was just holding back—because we're friends."

I was stunned.

"Then why didn't he get married?"

My mom sighed.

"Who says he didn't?
He was actually the first among us to marry.
But when his family fell into hard times,
he sent his wife back to her wealthy parents.

Life's strange like that.
The richest family's precious son in town
became the head of the household overnight.

If he managed to become a professor after that,
he must've suffered a great deal."

I had nothing left to say.

Only then did I understand
why the mockery of 'hysterical old bachelor'
had never really worked on him.

Embarrassed once again,
I kicked my blankets in silence
until I fell asleep.


Coke or Soy Sauce?

That day, my parents weren't home.

The professor came by and rang the doorbell.

I opened the door and said,
"My parents aren't home today~~"

He tilted his head.

"Huh? That's strange.

We agreed we'd make tteokbokki today.
Look—your mom texted me.
She said she'd have everything ready and told me to come by at four."

He showed me the message on his phone.

I checked my own messages,

then opened the refrigerator.

Sure enough,

all the ingredients for tteokbokki were there.

I called my mom.

"We had a minor fender bender, so we'll be late.

Darin, make tteokbokki for the professor, okay?"

And she hung up.

I had never cooked before.

Left with no choice, I pulled out my phone
and started following a recipe.

The professor watched for a moment, then said,

"Huh—if you do it like that, it won't taste very good."

I snapped back,

"Then you do it."

He calmly separated the rice cakes

and started moving around the kitchen,
busy with this and that.

I waited, thinking,

How different could it be from some famous franchise tteokbokki?

That's when my parents came home.

The professor greeted them cheerfully.

"Oh! You're late—later than the promised time!

The food's almost ready.
Have a seat!"

They laughed, washed their hands,

and joined us at the table.

For some reason,

the professor placed a portable gas burner
right in the middle of the table
and finished cooking the tteokbokki there.

He topped it with thinly sliced cabbage

and sprinkled pepper over it.

My dad smiled.

"This reminds me of what we used to eat

after school mixers back in middle school."

We each served ourselves.

I started eating with no expectations at all—

but after a few bites,
I realized something.

This was the best tteokbokki

I'd ever had.

After eating like maniacs,

we were all too full to move
and collapsed onto the sofa
and the living room floor.

As I lay there thinking,

People really aren't what they seem,
the professor walked over to the refrigerator.

He grabbed a plastic bottle,

twisted off the cap,
and took a big gulp.

My mom screamed.

"Hey!! That's not Coke—

that's soy sauce!!"

Only then did the professor pause.

"No wonder," he said thoughtfully.

"I thought the Coke tasted kind of salty."

He put the bottle down.

Our entire family burst out laughing.

The professor looked mildly embarrassed.

After he went home,

my mom asked casually,

"Darin, what do you think?

Wouldn't he make a good husband?"

I jumped up.

"Mom, are you crazy?

Do you know how big the age gap is?"

My dad chimed in,

"If he's that good of a man,

what does age matter?"

Completely flustered,

I retreated to my room.

Lying on my bed,

my thoughts started to wander.

Me... marrying the professor?

The moment I caught myself seriously considering it,

I felt utterly pathetic.

I kicked my blankets again

and eventually fell asleep.


Alien

When the winter break of my junior year ended, I became a senior.

My vague anxiety about student teaching and the teacher certification exam only grew stronger.

At the start of the new semester, I found out that an American professor had been newly appointed.

All I could think was, An American professor at a teachers' college? That's strange.

The new professor didn't teach any senior-level classes,

so I had no chance to meet her directly.

One day, I stopped by Professor KOD's office.

That was when I saw her.

Her hair wasn't the bright red I remembered from Anne of Green Gables,

nor was it the deep red of failed gochujang dye.

It was a faded, hard-to-describe color.

I didn't know what they had been talking about or why they stopped,

but there was a strange sense of laughter and warmth in the room.

Professor KOD said,

"Darin, this is Professor Maryann Jeksetic.

Maryann, this is my student, Gadarine. Say hello."

Caught off guard, I blurted out,

"Nice to meet you!"

Professor Maryann said something in return,

but whether she was greeting me

or insulting my looks,

I never managed to figure it out.

Professor KOD asked,

"So, Darin, what brings you here today?"

I answered,

"I'll tell you next time,"

and escaped the office as if I were running away.

Professors can talk to each other, I told myself at first.

But after that, the two of them were always together—

in the cafeteria,

around campus,

everywhere.

I believed that even professors should keep their romances after work,

but after that day,

the campus felt like a place I no longer belonged.

Later, I stopped by the teaching assistants' office.

"Lately, the professor doesn't seem very focused on research," I said.

The TA replied,

"How could he be? His fiancée from the U.S. is here."

I snapped back,

"Fiancée?

That old bachelor professor has a fiancée?"

The TA continued calmly,

"Apparently she's an Ivy League professor.

On top of that, she's the university president's daughter,

so she's well acquainted with our president too.

People are even saying Professor KOD might move to the U.S. soon."

I protested,

"There must be some misunderstanding.

What kind of charm does Professor KOD even have?"

The TA shook his head.

"You really don't know him, do you?

He's fairly well-known in academic circles.

If the president of that university came in person, that's a big deal.

He's probably received a scouting offer too."

I was speechless.

That old bachelor—such a clueless, foolish professor—

there's no way, I thought.

That day,

I attended my lectures,

ate my meals,

and went home,

but I remembered none of it.

House-Sharing

As soon as I got home, I asked my mom,

"I heard Professor KOD has a fiancée?"

She opened the refrigerator and answered casually,

"Oh? Could be.
Some classmates said they'd introduce someone to him, and he mentioned he already had a fiancée.
Guess he wasn't lying."

I frowned.

"How does KOD even date anyone~~?
What kind of charm does he even have~~~?"

Without turning around, Mom replied,

"Why wouldn't he?
He's way better than your dad.
Responsible, practical, and he can cook."

"I'm telling Dad."

"Go ahead.
He's not even your dad's rival. He won't care."

I had nothing to say.

The next day.

After class, I was heading to lunch alone when someone called out behind me.

"Darin!"

I turned around.

It was Professor Maryann.
KOD was standing beside her.

"If you're going to lunch, join us.
The faculty dining hall is a bit better, don't you think?
I'll treat."

I nodded.

The three of us were eating together when someone raised a hand from across the room.

It was the university president.

We all stood up at the same time.

"May I join you?"

Maryann smiled.

"Sure, of course."

The president sat down beside us naturally.

"How are you finding life in Korea?
Where do you live?
How do you like the accommodation?"

Maryann answered calmly.

"I chose house-sharing with Prof. John."

The president laughed loudly.

"An effective and economic idea!
Very impressive!
Professor John, you must take good care of your fiancée."

KOD said nothing.

He just smiled.

That smile was the most suspicious part.

That afternoon.

I opened my notebook.

At the top of the lecture page, I had written:

House-sharing
House-sharing
House-sharing

Circle.

Twice.

Three times.

If a man and a woman share a house...

Doesn't that mean they live together?

Then the kitchen too?

The living room too?

Then... the bedroom?

I dropped my pen.

Picked it up again.

House-sharing.

The letters seemed to grow larger and larger.

Back home, I lay on my bed.

I listed KOD's "charm points" one by one.

Cooking.
Practicality.
Responsibility.
That smile.

I buried my face in the pillow and kicked my blanket.

Once.

Twice.

Three times.

House-sharing.

The word floated around in my head
before slowly sinking somewhere deep.

And once again, for no reason at all,

I kicked the blanket—

and fell asleep.

Visiting

For days, I kept thinking about it.

House-sharing.

At first, it meant nothing.

If I turned to my left,
it became romance.

If I turned to my right,
it became something practical—
like my parents, just two people helping each other live.

And then other, more suggestive thoughts crept in.

At this rate, I was going to lose my mind.

No matter what,
I had to check it myself.

By coincidence, when I opened the kimchi refrigerator,
there were still several containers left from last winter.

Perfect.

This Saturday, I'd use the excuse that Mom wanted to deliver some kimchi
and go see for myself.

D–2.

A day that felt like a month.

D–1.

A day that felt like a year.

And finally—

D-day!!!

With the address Mom gave me,
I went to a two-story house in Myeonmok-dong.

The gate was open,
so I walked in and stood in front of the door,
just about to press the doorbell—

when I heard strange noises from inside.

Thud. Thud.

Heavy breathing.

And laughter.

I rang the bell.

Professor KOD opened the door,
his face covered in sweat.

As I stepped inside,
a wave of warm air hit me.

What are they doing in broad daylight—
I thought, marching in—

Only to see, on the living room TV,
Super Mario holding a tennis racket.

Maryann turned toward me,
panting,

"Do you wanna play tennis with me?"

She handed me a Joy-Con.

Just then—

the doorbell rang again.

Professor KOD went to open the door.

It was a delivery team.

They had come to install a bed.

Apparently, Maryann had ordered one.

She'd received a text saying it would arrive,
so they had left the front gate open.

One beer! One Kiss!

I suddenly felt ashamed of myself for having such ridiculous thoughts.

I declined the Joy-Con Maryann handed me

and passed over the container of kimchi instead.

"My mom said you should have this as a side dish," I muttered,

already preparing to flee.

But Professor KOD said,

"Stay for dinner.

We're making kimchi-jjim tonight."

I hesitated for half a second.

"Then... I'll just stay for dinner," I said,

sitting down on the sofa.

Once the delivery team finished installing the bed upstairs and left,

Professor KOD began cooking.

He took out two whole heads of kimchi

and rinsed them lightly under running water.

In a large pot, he boiled radish and vegetables,

skimmed the broth clean,
then diced pork belly and stir-fried it.

After that, he added the kimchi and seasoning

and let everything simmer.

Meanwhile, he placed three 200-gram chunks of beef in the oven

at 250°C.

About twenty minutes later,

the kimchi-jjim was bubbling vigorously.

He took the beef out,

cut it into cubes,
then put it back into the oven
at 400°C for another three minutes.

Maryann placed the kimchi-jjim in the center of the table

and skillfully plated the steak beside it.

Professor KOD came over with disposable gloves.

"You're supposed to tear kimchi-jjim with your hands," he said.

I was about to eat cautiously

when Maryann tore a long strip of kimchi,
wrapped a piece of steak inside it,
and held it out to me.

"Try this one!!!!"

I took the oversized bite awkwardly—

and froze.

I had never tasted kimchi-jjim like this.

The chewy texture of the kimchi,

the crisp sear on the steak,
the juicy tenderness inside—

it exploded in my mouth.

We kept eating.

Then Maryann brought out soju.

We poured and shared drinks

and started talking.

She began telling stories about her time in the U.S.

"One day," she said,

"we were cooking dinner with friends.
We'd just bought groceries,
and Professor KOD said to me—"

She mimicked his voice.

"I wanna buy you beer."

"OK!"

"But just one condition—

One beer, one kiss!"

She laughed.

"I thought it was hilarious, so I said—

'Not too much.'"

I didn't know whether to be shocked or amused.

So I laughed.

The kimchi-jjim was incredible.

We ate too much.
We drank too much.

Professor KOD eventually called my dad.

"Come pick up your daughter."

An hour later,

my dad arrived and took me home.

In the car,

the alcohol started to wear off.

Lying in bed,

I murmured to myself:

"One eer. One kiss."

If one beer is one kiss...

Then two beers...

Three beers...

I kicked my blanket and turned over.

But still—

The kimchi-jjim had been really, really good.


Mission Impossible


I made up my mind.

I would stop caring about Professor KOD.

So for several days, I went back and forth between my house and the library, carrying stacks of major textbooks.

Students from other departments were writing graduation theses, creating projects, preparing exhibitions.

But in the math department, there was only one option—

exams.

Even seniors said that writing a proper thesis was difficult, even in graduate school.

I thought I was working hard.

But it felt like walking in fog.

And so, I had no choice but to accept what Professor KOD had once said.

Maybe I really didn't have talent.

One day, feeling completely crestfallen, I was walking past the library when I heard—

"Daaaarin~~~"

It was Professor Maryann.

She still can't pronounce Korean properly, I thought.

"Yes, hello," I answered flatly.

She tilted her head.

"Why do you look so drained today?"

I just pouted silently.

She smiled.

"Studying feels hard these days, doesn't it?
Feels like you're working, but not getting any better?"

My eyes widened.

"How did you know that?"

She laughed softly.

"Because I felt the same way."

I blinked.

"You? Without talent?"

She nodded.

"Your KOD professor once told me the same thing.
'Maryann, you have no talent for mathematics.'"

I felt indignant.

"He is a son of—"

She cut me off gently.

"When I told John I wanted to give up because I didn't think I had talent,
he said there was only one way to find out whether I did or not.

He asked if I was willing to try.

Of course I said yes."

I leaned in.

"And then?"

"The next day," she said calmly,
"he took me to a bungee jumping site.
Fifty meters high."

I froze.

"He told me to jump.

I gave up three times.

Then John said he'd go first.

I was standing next to him.

The moment the staff started counting down—

he suddenly grabbed me and jumped."

She laughed.

"I screamed every curse I knew.
'Shit! Asshole!!!'"

"After we were brought back to the platform and unhooked,
John handed me a strawberry candy and said—

'Welcome to Mission Impossible — Math.'"

She looked at me quietly.

"Later he told me something.

Where in the world are there people born with talent for mathematics?

We're all just walking the path that geniuses have already cleared.

That's when I realized—

he struggles too.

John thinks he has no talent either."

I stared at her.

"That arrogant, confident professor?
He thinks he has no talent?"

She smirked.

"A genius doesn't pee in a refrigerator."

I blinked.

"In... your refrigerator too?"

She nodded.

"He had no money back then.

He kept apologizing, saying he couldn't afford to replace it.

So I told him—

when he becomes a professor,
he can replace the refrigerator with an engagement ring."

I swallowed.

"You liked someone like that?"

She smiled.

"I thought—
at least life would never be boring with this man."

She began walking away.

"Oh, and Darin—
from now on, when it's just the two of you,
call me by my name.

You share a secret now, don't you?"

And just like that, she left.

Only then did I begin to understand Professor KOD a little more.

But that day—

I still thought about him.

All day.

Love Letter

One day, the campus became unusually noisy.

People were whispering about an Ivy League university president visiting,
about overseas dignitaries arriving.

I wasn't particularly interested.

That was an administrative issue.
Not my business.

But a few days later,

while I was having lunch in the cafeteria with Maryann and Professor KOD,
the university president waved and approached us.

Beside him stood an elderly white professor.

"May we join you?"

We shifted to make room.

In the middle of the meal, the president asked Maryann,

"How did the two of you meet?"

Maryann smiled.

"I was studying in the library.
A student came by and handed me a sheet of paper."

Then she read slowly:

I guess I'm not good at keeping love for long.
I think I found the answer, but the answer is always wrong.

"I thought it was a love letter," she said.
"So I ignored it."

My chopsticks froze mid-air.

She continued,

"But a week passed.
Then a month.

And that student never said anything.

So I asked him first.

'If you sent a love letter, shouldn't you at least ask me out for coffee?'"

The president laughed.

"And then?"

Maryann grinned.

"He looked confused and said,

'Love letter?
That was just something I wrote while struggling with a proof.
It wouldn't resolve, so I compared mathematics to love.'"

I turned to look at KOD.

He had no expression at all.

Maryann continued.

"When I asked why he gave it to me,
he said,

'I thought you were in the same lecture.
Just wanted to cheer you up.'

Still, he bought me coffee.

That's how we became close."

The president muttered,

"KOD never even realizes what he's done."

The elderly professor beside him spoke quietly.

"Last year, he visited our university and scribbled something on a blackboard.

It's now been submitted as a Fields Medal candidate paper.

A talent like this... requires supervision."

Maryann and I spoke at the same time.

"Exactly.
He's dangerous. He needs supervision."

The old professor nodded solemnly.

"Then perhaps you could send him to our university.
We'll make sure humanity suffers no damage."

The president turned to KOD.

"And what do you think?"

Just as KOD was about to speak,

the elderly professor added casually,

"The young man living with my daughter sure talks a lot.
He should hurry up and get married and move into our house."

In that moment,

KOD said nothing.

After the meal, I asked Maryann quietly,

"That man earlier..."

"My father."

"The president?"

"Mm."

That's when I realized.

These people
do not live in the same world as I do.

I muttered under my breath,

"What kind of humans even are they..."

And yet—

that sentence from the letter
would not leave my mind.

I found the answer.
But the answer is always wrong.

It wasn't a love letter.

Which made it

the most dangerous sentence of all.


Joker


After that, Maryann and I began having lunch together regularly.
When we ate at the faculty cafeteria, Professor KOD and the philosophy professor often joined us.

One day, the four of us were eating when Maryann suddenly burst out laughing and said loudly,

"Yesterday, KOD slept in my bed!"

The entire cafeteria turned to look at us.

I froze, not knowing where to put my eyes.

KOD replied calmly,

"I bought the bed, so it's not your bed—it's my bed.
And I only lay down to check if it had arrived properly. I just happened to fall asleep."

Everyone around us looked stunned.

Maryann only smiled brightly.

I felt miserable, eating lunch with these shameless people.

A few days later, I stopped by Maryann's office and found her in a serious argument with KOD.

They were debating what to eat for lunch.

Whether to eat
ramyeon with kimbap,
or
kimbap with ramyeon.

They argued about this nonsense for an entire hour.

In the end, they ordered pizza.

After eating, I went for a walk with Maryann and asked,

"I don't understand how Professor KOD can act so out of context all the time.
Ramyeon with kimbap, kimbap with ramyeon—it's basically the same thing, isn't it?"

Maryann laughed.

"It's slightly different!
It's about choosing the main dish and the side dish.
The main stays the same, but you can switch the side. That's the point."

I frowned.

"If you already know that, why even argue about it?"

She smiled.

"KOD just likes turning boring things into something interesting.
Math people can seem a little crazy, but they try to treat situations like variables—like puzzles to solve logically and playfully."

I couldn't understand.

"But why argue about something that makes no sense?"

Maryann shrugged.

"I didn't understand at first either.

But after I broke up with KOD, married other men, and lived a 'stable' life...
I realized something.

They were all predictable. Structured. Safe.

Eventually, conversation disappeared.
Life became dull.
I even went through depression.

It wasn't until later that I understood—

living according to a framework defined by someone else
makes you feel stagnant.

So I came back.

When I'm with KOD, I feel alive.

And that bed comment the other day?
It probably vanished from everyone's minds because of the ramyeon–kimbap debate."

I still didn't fully understand.

But I had to admit—

those two were inseparable.

And yet...

for some reason,

I still found myself kicking my blankets that night.


With one look


Maryann and Professor KOD said they were leaving.

Their final farewell party would be with our family.

Mom and Dad spent all Saturday morning cooking and cleaning.

"Why are you making japchae and even sinseollo for a simple farewell dinner?"
I complained.

Mom answered calmly,

"He replaced our refrigerator, didn't he?
Your stingy father hadn't changed it in twenty years.
Honestly, I think he caused that accident on purpose.
We went to school together for at least ten years.
There's nothing we don't know about each other."

That evening, Maryann and KOD arrived with a bottle of wine and champagne.

KOD said,

"Hey, I said let's keep it simple.
Why did you prepare all this?"

Dad laughed.

"You've come out in the middle of the night several times because of my drunk daughter."

My face burned.
I pinched Dad's side.

He continued,

"At least we got to reconnect with an old elementary school friend!
Your professor even told me not to mention we were friends.
Said you might get misunderstood at school."

Embarrassed, I shot back,

"That's why he put me through senior hazing!"

Everyone burst out laughing.

Maryann and Mom watched our banter with amusement.

After dinner, we went to karaoke.

I started first.
Maryann sang a song too.

KOD searched for a long time before selecting one.

An old cartoon theme song began to play.

"Beyond the blue sea, the waves are rolling..."

The moment he started singing,
Mom and Dad jumped up and stood beside him,
throwing their arms over his shoulders and singing together.

They looked like elementary school kids joyfully shouting in chorus.

For the first time,
I felt like I was seeing my parents' childhood.

We sang for nearly an hour and a half,
until everyone was exhausted.

Then KOD selected another song.

He began softly,

"I guess I'm not good at keeping love for long.
I think I found the answer but the answer is always wrong."

Maryann and I looked at each other.

"Love letter," we said at the same time.

He continued,

"Next time you fall in love it'd better with me.
Back then was when we touched the starlight."

When the song ended,
KOD knelt in front of Maryann
and took out a purple ring box.

"It's late," he said quietly.
"But...
Would you marry me?"

Maryann wiped her tears.

"Yes."

They kissed.

KOD smiled and added,

"With one first look,
I found the answer.
You."

I was about to say,
"Professor, from the very beginning—"

but Mom and Dad dragged me out.

That was the last time I saw them.

I didn't feel the need to go to the airport.

All this time,
I had just been kicking my blankets over nothing.

Still—

it felt good.

Even if it was someone else's romance,
it made my heart flutter.


Epilogue

One day, while studying in the library,

a male junior approached and handed me a note.

It read:

"Sunbae,
I always think I've found the answer,
but it always turns out to be wrong."

I'd seen that sentence before.

I folded the note and slipped it into my bag.

Maybe—

my life
was about to become interesting too.
